newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: PRESS DIGEST - NZ Business weeklies - May 2.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - NZ Business weeklies - May 2.

text.p: Billion-dollar tobacco industry faces lawsuit: New Zealand's $1 billion a year tobacco industry is gearing up its legal machine as it faces the first local class action alleging personal injury from smoking. Page 1.
Public rejects privatisation: The benefits of privatisation to consumers and the economy may be obvious to most businesspeople but the majority doesn't want to know. Page 1.
Super scheme threatens tax take: Confidential cabinet papers reveal the proposed compulsory superannuation scheme threatens government revenue and spending targets. Page 1.
Mogul's yacht languishes in dry dock after hitting reef: Auckland might not be the favoured port of call for mega tycoon Kerry Packer to spend $5 million getting his boat fixed after all. Page 3.
Fay Fichwhite faces hefty tax bill: Merchant bank Fay Richwhite & Co may face a $2.3 million bill after its tax-driven investment deals through a third party ran foul of Inland Revenue. Page 3.

Hard task for merino marketers cracking the Italian rag trade: The fledging organisation set up to market New Zealand's merino wool may be forced to defile its pure fibre with synthetics if it wants to win over the Armanis and Gaultiers of the fashion world. Page 6.

Energy firm more than just wind: Turbine technology moves up a gear and brings Vortec closer to US listing: The flick of a switch next Wednesday will set in motion new energy technology that could create a billion dollar international business for its New Zealand backers. Page 7.

Lease companies losers as car prices plummet: The massive price war in the car market has seen vehicles depreciate so steeply that lease companies are likely to be out of pocket on three-year operating leases expiring this year. Page 9.

BIL lines up to join attack on wine-box commissioner: Brierly Investments looks set to join Fay Richwhite & Co in its marathon attack on the fairness of wine-box commissioner Sir Ronald Davison. Page 10.
Ministers can't see the wood for trees: Two government members on either side of the Coalition are divided over the use of indigenous native forests on the West Coast. Page 10.

Compulsory superannuation scheme attracts opposition from everywhere: An extraordinary coalition of groups normally on opposite ends of the political spectrum has formed against the government's proposed compulsory superannuation scheme. Page 12.
New Zealand escapes being named on US trade hit list: The powerful US pharmaceutical lobby has failed to have New Zealand punished for its drug-buying policies. Page 13.

Reef's rescue too late as Searoad drowns in debt: Coastal shipper Searoad has gone in liquidation just seven days after a Reef Group-led consortium announced it was trying to buy the company. Page 13.

Maoris find loophole in land law: To buy the former Wigram airbase, Ngai Tahu set up a special airport company called Wigram Aerodrome, which circumvented the Public Works Act offer-back provisions on surplus Crown land. Page 14.

Loss of face will be price of failure to upgrade defence: The government will this year have to make the hard decisions on defence spending it has avoided since the Bolger administration came to power in 1990. Page 15.

Japan praises defence stance but trade barrier still solid: The government got no promises of an early cut in continuing barriers to trade during the Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto's visit to Wellington this week -- but unexpected praise for a perceived move back into the Western security alliance. Page 17.
